document.title: Purification of Sour Cherry Necrotic Ringspot and Prune Dwarf Viruses'

method.heading: MATERIALS AND METHODS
method.text:
The cherry nevrotic ringspot and prune dwarf viruses were the same isolates referred to in previous investigations as virus G andvirus B, respectively (Fulton, 1957a, 1957c). Virus G caused necrotic ringspot when inoculated to sour cherry (Fulton, 1958). More recently, virus B has caused typical prune dwarf symptoms when inoculat'ed to Italian Prune (Prunus domestica L.) and has caused symptoms nearly identical t#o illustrations (Willison et al., 1951) of tatter leaf of sweet cherry (P. &urn L.). Neither virus separately, nor a combination of the t'wo, has caused sour cherry yellows.
,&ays showed that extracts of cucumber cotyledons (Cucumis sativus 1,. var. Improved Chicago Pickling) inoculated with necrotic ringspot virus were maximally infectious 3-6 days after inoculation, and t,hat such tissue contained a higher concentration of virus than ot,her hosts investigated. Inoculated cucumber cotyledons were therefore used as a source of necrotic ringspot virus.
Although the time required to reach a maximum concemration in cucumber cotyledons varied seasonally, virus content could be judged roughly from the degree of yellowing of the cotyledons. If these failed to become uniformly yellow within 6 days, or showed only isolat,ed yellow lesions, the virus content was invariably low. In late spring, necrotic ringspot virus usually remained in low concentration in cucumber cotyledons. This appeared to be due to environmental conditions prior to inoculation, as incubation of inoculated plants under controlled conditions failed to result in increased virus concentrat'ions.
The hydrated calcium phosphate (HCP) used to adsorb host material was prepared by adding to a 0.1 N solution of Na2HP04 slightly less than an equal volume of 0.1 M CaClz . The flocculent white precipitate settled enough in 1-6 hours to allow one-third or more of the supernatant to be decamed. Distilled water was added and t'he precipit'ate resuspended. Decantation and resuspension of the precipitate in dist,illed water was done fifteen to twenty times to remove soluble salts.
After washing, the HCP was packed by centrifuging at, low speed. The final preparation was about the consistency of soft but'ter and had a water content of 97 %. It was stored in this form at room temperature. The gel-like consistency and the ability to adsorb green plant' material were lost after drying and resuspending in water.
Most of the work reported here was done with the necrotic ringspot virus. The method of purification developed for this virus was then applied to the prune dwarf virus in inoculated cucumber cotyledons. The presence of virus in preparations resulting from various steps in the purification procedure was checked by infectivity assays. Local lesion assay hosts used were Momordica balsamina L. for necrotic ringspot virus and Sesbania ezaltata (Raf.) Cory for prune dwarf virus. Carborundum was used for all inoculations. Virus preparations were diluted with 0.02 or 0.03 M pH 8.0 phosphate buffer for inoculation.

document.full_text:
Necrotic ringspot and prune dwarf viruses are very commonly found infecting sour cherries (Prunus cerasus I,.). Their differentiation is important because each may be carried without symptoms in sour cherry. Each has been suspected of being a contributing factor to diseases which may result from the presence of a second virus in infected trees.
Each of these two viruses can be identified by characteristic reactions of differential Prunus hosts on graft inoculation (Berkeley et al., 1951;Hildebrand et al., 1951), or more rapidly by mechanical inoculation to differential herbaceous hosts (Fulton, 1957a). Neither of these methods of identification, however, eliminates the possibility of confusion with other unrelat'ed viruses which might induce similar symptoms. It appeared that more precise identification would be possible if necrot,ic ringspot' and prune dwarf viruses could be concentrated and purified, their sizes and shapes det'ermined, and the possibility explored of using purified preparations as antigens.
Both viruses are very unstable in undiluted plant extracts and lose most of their infectivity within a few minutes. Various chemicals have been found, however, which are effective in stabilizing infectivity of prune dwarf virus (lulton, 1957c). h treatment which stabilized bot'h viruses, and which appeared promising as an initial step in purification, consisted of grinding infected tissue in 20925 volumes of 0.03 M pH 8.0 phosphate containing l-2 volumes of hydrated calcium phosphate (l'ulton, 1957b). Most of bhe chloroplast'ic material and cell debris adsorbed to the gel-like calcium phosphate and sedimented readily on low speed centrifugation. The viruses remained in t'he nearly waterclear supernatant and retained their infectivit'y for several days.
The stability of t'he viruses in calcium phosphat,e-treated extract's indicated that some Cssue constituent was responsible for the apparent, i&ability of the viruses. It, seemed probable that purified virus would be sufficiently stable for use as an ant,igen in serological investigat'ions. Such material also would be useful in det,ermining the nat,ure of inactivation occurring in tissue extract's
In previous electron microscopical investigations, Willison et al. (1956) presented evidence bhat necrotic ringspot virus is a sphere about' 40 rnp in diameter and that prune dwarf virus is a SO-rnp sphere. Thornberry (1958) reported isolatjing viruslike particles 80 rnp in diameter from tissue infected with cherry ringspot. These reports appear conflicting, but may not have dealt wit,h the same viruses, since in neither case was the material isolated shown to cause the typical disease in stone fruits.

Virus G caused necrotic ringspot when inoculated to sour cherry (Fulton, 1958). Most of the work reported here was done with the necrotic ringspot virus. The method of purification developed for this virus was then applied to the prune dwarf virus in inoculated cucumber cotyledons. The presence of virus in preparations resulting from various steps in the purification procedure was checked by infectivity assays. Local lesion assay hosts used were Momordica balsamina L. for necrotic ringspot virus and Sesbania ezaltata (Raf.) Cory for prune dwarf virus. Carborundum was used for all inoculations. Virus preparations were diluted with 0.02 or 0.03 M pH 8.0 phosphate buffer for inoculation.
As reported previously (E'ulton, 1957b), adsorption of virus and host mnt'erial on HCP was differentially affected by the ionic concentration of the homogenate. This was determined by homogenizing infected tissue in 25 volumes of phosphate buffer containing 2.5 volumes of HCP and centrifuging. When the buffer concentration was below about 0.006 M both virus and green host material adsorbed to the HCP, leaving a clear, nearly noninfectious supernatant. The presence of virus in the green sediment was demonstrated by resuspending it in 0.04 M buffer and cent,rifuging again. At this buffer concentration, green host material remained adsorbed to HCP and was sedimented. The virus, however, as shown by infectivity tests given in Table 1, appeared in the clear supernatant.
For the purpose of clarification a buffer concentration of 0.03 M appeared optimal. Aft'er centrifugat'ion of homogenates of infected tissue and HCP in buffer of this concentration a nearly water-clear supernat,ant was obtained which was usually more infectious t,han control preparations without HCP. Moreover, necrot'ic ringspot virus remained infectious in such supernatants for several days at room temperat,ure. Although stabilization of necrotic ringspot virus was obbained by homogenization with 25 volumes of buffer containing HCP, centrifugal concentration of virus from such large volumes was impractical. When more concentrated homogenates were prepared, containing infected tissue, buffer, and HCP in a w:v:v proportion of 10: 15: 12, good clarification usually was obtained only if the concentration of the buffer used was below 0.03 M. Apparently the amount of soluble electrolyt,es contributed to the homogenate by the tissue was sufficient to raise t,he total salt concentration beyond the point where green bissue constituents would adsorb. Lower buffer concentrations resulted in more nearly complete clarification. Good clarification was obtained by homogenizing 10 g of cucumber cotyledons, 15 ml of 0.02 31 buffer, and 12 ml HCP and centrifuging.
Virus stability often was poor in the more concentrated homogenates, despite what appeared to be excellent removal of green plant, constituents. A few preparations retained most of their original infectivity for 6-8 hours; many became nearly completely noninfectious within 2-3 hours. After it was found (Hampton and Fulton, 1959) that necrotic ringspot virus infectivity could be stabilized by including 0.01 M sodium diethyldithiocarbamate in extracts, this compound was used to maintain infectivity.
Sodium thioglycolate also was included routinely with both viruses, although a mixture of the two compounds was essential in maintaining infectivity of only the prune dwarf virus. Keibher sodium diethyldithiocarbamate nor sodium thioglycolate at concentrations up to 0.05 M affected adsorption of green material to the HCP.
After virus stabilization was obtained with chemical additives it was found that less HCP was needed for clarificat'ion when large tissue fragments were first removed from homogenates by low speed centrifugation. The procedure used for clarification therefore was to homogenize infected tissue in a Waring blendor with a solution of 0.01 &I sodium diethyldithiocarbamate and 0.02 M sodium thioglycolate in 0.02 N pH 8.0 phosphate buffer, using 15 ml of solution for each 10 g of tissue. Dow Corning Antifoam A was used to reduce foaming. The homogenate was cent,rifuged at 2500 rpm for 15 minutes. HCP was added to the supernatant, at the rate of 6 ml for each 10 g of original tissue, and the mat,erials were mixed by drawing them into and expelling them from a large syringe fitted with a glass tube instead of a needle. Foaming was reduced by keeping the tip of the tube below the surface of the liquid. This mixture then was centrifuged at 2500 rpm for 15 minutes. One treat,ment wit]h HCP removed nearly all green material from the homogenate. Mixing the supernatant a second time with HCP, using half the volume of the first treatment, usually removed an additional small amount of green material, leaving a clear amber supernatant. No attempt was made t,o keep virus-containing extracts cold, except that homogenization was done in a cold room at 5" C.
Following clarification, the virus-containing extracts were centrifuged 20 minutes at 10,000 rpm. This apparently only served to remove traces of HCP which were not removed at lower speed. Virus then was pelleted by centrifugat,ion in a Spinco model L ultracentrifuge for 2 hours at 30,000 rpm in a no. 30 rotor. The pellets were composed of a clear glassy portion and a smaller portion of tan-colored insoluble material.
The high speed pellets were resuspended in 0.02 M pH 8.0 phosphate buffer by 15-20 minutes' gentle shaking on a mechanical shaker. When resuspended in distilled mater, pellets had much lower infectivity t)han in buffer. The resuspended pellets were centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 20 minutes; this removed most of the opaque port'ion of the original pellet. Virus was sedimented again by centrifuging 2 hours in a Spinro no. 40 rotor at 35,000 rpm. The resulting pellets were nearly colorless, and opayue material was reduced to, at most, a small dot in t)he cent,er of the pellet. Most of this was removed by subsequent centrifugation for 20 minutes at, 10,000 rpm.
The final pellet suspensions in 0.02 M pH 8.0 phosphate buffer usually represented a ten-to twentyfold concentration of virus, assuming complete recovery. Such suspensions were infectious at dilutions of 1: 1000 or more, and comparative assays showed that they contained between 50 and 100 % of the original infectivity. The accuracy of these comparisons was probably low, however, because samples of tissue retained for assays may not have represented accurately the entire lot of Gssue. Undiluted purified virus preparations infected stone fruit seedlings readily. Typical symptoms of necrotic ringspot were produced on -4 of 4 sour cherry seedlings inoculated with one preparation of necrotic ringspot virus.
Virus was prepared for electron microscopy by diluting purified preparations 1 : 10 to 1: 30 in water or 0.002 M pH 8.0 phosphate buffer. Dilutions greater than 1: 10 in distilled water were generally unsatisfactory, as particles appeared aggregated in clumps of various sizes. Polystyrene latex spheres of an average diameter of 122.5 rnp were included in all preparations. The diluted virus was sprayed on collodion films supported by electron microscope screen disks and air-dried. After being shadowed with uranium they were viewed in an RCA EMU2 electron microscope. Necrotic ringspot virus appeared to consist of uniform, apparently round particles (Fig. 1,A). Measurements were made from images of electron micrographs projected on a screen. In comparison with the size of the polystyrene latex spheres the average size of fifty virus particles was 23.5 mp. There was 25-30 % variation in measured widths of individual particles, much of which was probably due to their small size and to indistinctness of the image margins at high magnification. Similar preparations of prune dwarf virus consisted of particles averaging 22.3 rnp in diameter (Fig. 1,B).
The polystyrene spheres in these preparations cast "shadows" 1.5 to 1.7 times their width. The virus particles, on the other hand, cast "shadows" shorter than their widths. Assuming that the virus when suspended in liquid was isodiametric, it appeared to have been much flattened as a result of drying, which would result in apparent diameters greater t,han the actual diameters.
In an attempt to reduce flattening, virus dilutions were sprayed on electron microscope grids in contact with metal at solid COZ temperature and the ice was sublimed by applying a vacuum to the grids in a sealed container. Such frozen-dried necrotic ringspot virus averaged 20.6 rnp in diameter, and prune dwarf virus averaged 20.0 mp. Even in these preparations, however, the ratio of "shadow" length to part,icle width was less for virus than for the polystyrene spheres. Whether this discrepancy was due to measurement errors related to the small size of the virus particles on an apparently rough surface or to some other cause is not known.
Purified preparations appeared to consist almost entirely of a suspension of uniform particles. The reduction in extract volume obtained during purification yielded preparations which were proportionately more infectious than was the same volume of infected tissue extract. It seemed probable therefore that the particles represented the infect'ive units. On a number of electron micrographs, particles larger than the typical size were found. Most of these were rather clearly aggregates of two particles, with their adjacent sides somewhat flattened. Others appeared, although less distinctly, to be clumps of three or more particles.
Other evidence indicated also that the typical particles represented virus. When healthy cucumber cotyledons were processed in the same way as infected tissue, only small opaque pellets were obtained by high speed centrifugation of the HCP-treated supernatant; no clear glassy material was present. No visible material was pelleted by the second high speed centrifugation.
The behavior of infective material in adsorbing to and eluting from HCP in response to changes in ionic strength suggested an additional correlation between the presence of typical particles and the presence of infectivity. Electron microscopic observation of HCP showed that it was composed of very thin platelets which were surprisingly transparent' to the electron beam (Fig. 2,A). Purified virus in 0.02 Jf phosphate buffer was diluted 1 : 10 in distilled water containing HCP. At the ionic skength The characteristic particles of necrotic ringspot virus behaved ill the same way as the infective material, and appeared or1 or near the HCl' in 0.002 M buffer (E'ig. 2, R). The few particles whicah did not remain in c*ontacat, with HCI' may have 'Lesc:Lped" when sufficient water evaporat,ed to raise the ionic c.onc,ent,ration in the region of the HCI'. I':trtic*lcs suspended in 0.03 W buffer, OII t,he other hand, remained free of HCl' except for the few which might be expected if they were randomly distrihutcd (Fig. 2,C). I'urified preparations diluted 1: 10 in distilled water to give a buffer concentration of 0.002 M and stored for I week at 2' were less than 10 % as infectious as similar dilutions in 0.03 M buffer. Both preparations were furt'her diluted in 0.03 M buffer for inoculation. Concentrated purified preparations in 0.02 M pH 8.0 phosphate buffer have remained infectious at 2" for 65 days, the longest period tested. It was evident, however, that they were less infectious t'han when freshly prepared.
Purified virus was very readily inactivated by vigorous shaking to induce foaming. In one trial, virus in 0.03 M buffer shaken vigorously by hand for 2 minutes gave 6 lesions on three half-leaves. A preparation identical except for t'he presence of 1 % gelatin induced 54 lesions after shaking. The unshaken control produced 100 lesions. One attempt to resuspend virus pelleted at 80,000 g by shaking it vigorously resulted in the appearance of a whitish coagulum and the complete loss of infectivity.
In general no data obtained indicat'ed any major differences between the two Prunus viruses and the more thoroughly studied viruses of herbaceous plan& The sizes of the Prunus viruses place them among the smaller plant viruses. Their instability appears to be the result of a marked sensitivity to certain host components in extracts. Once these are removed or inhibited, stability of the viruses is increased to a point roughly comparable wit,h the stabilities of such viruses as cucumber mosaic or tobacco ringspot.
Stabilization of extract infectivity by sodium diethyldithiocarbamate and sodium thioglycolate raised a question regarding the necessity of using HCP for clarification.
A few preparations were treated with quantities of HCP insufficient to remove all green color. Two cycles of high and low speed centrifugation failed to remove all the green color from the pellets. It seemed clear that the relatively simple and rapid clarification with HCP facilitated subsequent centrifugal concentration and purification.
The possibility of using HCP for other steps in addition to initial clarification was investigated. Its use in a chromatographic column was impractical because of extremely slow flow rates. Attempts to concentrate virus by adsorbing it on HCP from dilute extracts and then eluting with small quantities of buffer gave poor yields. There appeared to be a rather rapid loss of virus infectivity at ionic concentrations at which virus adsorbed to HCP. Furthermore, quantitative elution of adsorbed virus required successive washings wit'h a total volume of buffer approaching the volume of the original extract.
Although the yield of virus from a known weight of tissue was not determined, it was quite evident from the small size of the pellets that the amount, of virus obtained was less than that obtained with many ot,her plant viruses. Infectivity comparisons did not indicate any major loss of virus during purification.
It appeared therefore that' the two Prunus viruses exert t.heir rather severe pathological effects in cucumber without reaching a concentration comparable with that of many plant viruses.
The diameters of necrotic ringspot and prune dwarf viruses found in this investigation were markedly less than those reported by Willison r:t al. (1956) or by Thornberry (1958). The differences appear t'oo large to he due to variations in technique, in spite of numerous possible sources of error in making precise electron microscopic measurements. It is possible that different viruses were measured in each case. Thornberry's preparations were report,edly noninfective and could have COINtained particles which were a product of disease rather than it,s cause. Willison et al. determined sizes on the basis of an increase in the proport)ion of particles in certain size ranges in infected tissue as compared to healthy tissue. These also could have been products of deranged host met)abolism rather t,han virus. Or they could have been aggregates of smaller particles.
